analysis.one_liner: Requires emergency-department hospitals in the 340B drug discount program to provide sexual assault forensic care or safe transfers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee until the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Hospitals with emergency rooms that buy discounted drugs through the federal 340B program would have to become 'SAFE-ready' — meaning a trained sexual assault forensic examiner is available or on call 24/7 — within two years, or follow strict interim rules: tell victims they are not a SAFE-ready facility, point them to the nearest one, and transfer them there free of charge with the victim's written consent. Hospitals that fail to comply could lose their 340B drug discounts.
analysis.who_benefits: Sexual assault victims who arrive at a hospital emergency department. Today, many emergency departments have no sexual assault forensic examiner available, so victims may not be offered a proper medical-forensic exam or evidence collection. The bill would either make a trained examiner available around the clock or guarantee victims are informed of their options and moved, at no cost, to a hospital that can examine them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Sexual assault victims at hospital ERs

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals with emergency departments in the 340B program must employ or contract with sexual assault forensic examiners available 24 hours a day, every day, to earn a SAFE-ready designation [S3].

Hospitals that are not yet SAFE-ready must inform victims, provide the location of the nearest SAFE-ready facility, and offer free stabilization and transfer by the hospital's own transportation, with the victim's written consent and confirmation that an examiner is available at the receiving hospital [S3].
The Secretary of Health and Human Services must publish and annually update a public list of designated SAFE-ready facilities, so victims and advocates can find them [S3].
Continued participation in the 340B discount program is conditioned on becoming SAFE-ready or meeting the interim requirements, giving hospitals a financial reason to comply [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The 340B hospitals themselves — disproportionate-share, rural, and other safety-net hospitals that rely on the drug discounts. They would bear the cost of hiring or contracting forensic examiners, staff training plans, and free patient transfers, and could lose their 340B eligibility if they fail. Taxpayers are not directly charged; the enforcement lever is the hospitals' existing drug discount.

drawbacks.text: Recruiting sexual assault forensic examiners for 24/7 coverage is difficult and expensive, especially for small rural hospitals, and the bill gives them only two years to comply before risking loss of 340B eligibility [S3].

Requiring hospitals to confirm examiner availability and arrange official transportation for each transfer could add administrative steps in an emergency setting, and the no-cost transfer obligation falls on safety-net hospitals already operating on thin margins [S3].
The bill only reaches hospitals in the 340B program; emergency departments outside it would face no new duty to provide or arrange forensic exams.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to victims — a real option for a proper forensic exam, either on site or through a guaranteed free transfer — is significant and targeted at a moment of acute need. The costs fall on a defined group of hospitals that in exchange receive deeply discounted drugs, and the two-year runway plus an interim notification-and-transfer regime is a reasonable ramp. The main honest concern is whether every affected hospital can actually staff 24/7 examiner coverage in two years; the interim rules partially soften that by ensuring victims are at least directed to care elsewhere.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never held a hearing or markup on it, and it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mimi Walters (R-CA) introduced the bill on June 28, 2018, with Rep. Greg Walden (R-OR) joining as an original co-sponsor [S1] [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S5].
Four Republican members cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
No further action was taken — no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals in the 340B program are better off: they keep their discounted drugs without any new obligation to staff sexual assault forensic examiners or guarantee transfers for victims.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: 340B hospitals keep discounts, no new duties

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat ever signed on, and no vote was ever taken to test broader support.

industries.note: The bill conditions hospitals' continued access to discounted 340B drugs on staffing 24/7 sexual assault forensic examiners or meeting interim notification-and-transfer rules, a real cost these hospitals would otherwise avoid. Hospitals' interest in keeping the discounts without the new care obligations runs against victims' interest in getting examined.
